item.title: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
item.description:
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration on Wednesday over its campaign-style ads.

Why it matters: The DNC alleges the ads, which have drawn considerable backlash as they were originally paid for with taxpayer money, violate several federal laws.

What they're saying: "These ads are a clear violation of the Congressional ban on the use of appropriated funds for 'publicity or propaganda purposes,'" the DNC's legal counsel wrote in the lawsuit.

  • "The president has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day 'midterm convention,' and repeatedly directed voters to 'pretend that I am on the ballot," it added.
  • "As the 2026 midterm election has approached, Republican poll numbers have plummeted in both traditional battlegrounds and typically favorable states, and Democrats are poised to take control of Congress, governors' mansions, and state legislatures around the country."
  • Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Zoom in: The lawsuit alleges the White House crafted the ads to boost the president's approval ratings and help Republican candidates.

  • The complaint largely focuses on its allegation that the ads were paid for with money originally allocated for Customs and Border Protection that was rerouted for the TV spots.
  • The DNC argues that the ads violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the Antideficiency Act, and the Purpose Act.

The DNC asked a federal judge to step in, declare the administration's actions illegal and immediately block them from airing any more ads paid for with taxpayer money.

  • It's not clear how the judge will rule, given President Trump said Monday that a Trump-affiliated super PAC would begin paying for the ads moving forward.
  • A White House spokesperson confirmed Tuesday to Axios that the administration would not repay the government for the ads.

Catch up quick: According to the suit, Trump personally hand-picked the ads that aired on television, which were broadcast to millions of Americans, including during NFL and college football games.

  • The lawsuit says the ads aired "nearly 90 times across national television networks, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now, and CBS" over four days in late September. Those spots likely cost around $337,000.
  • In that same time period, the ads aired on local television stations at least 2,311 times and those placements cost around $1.4 million, the suit says.
  • Advertisement tracking firm AdImpact estimates that over $2.5 million was spent on the ads the first week they were aired.

Worth noting: Using public funds for campaign ads hasn't sat well with American voters.

  • Nearly nine in ten voters said in a Reuters-Ipsos poll published Wednesday that using taxpayer money for campaign ads featuring a president or Cabinet member is inappropriate.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up

Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

item.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
item.description:
The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier.

The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say.

  • Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response.
  • "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios.
  • A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time.
  • "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."
  • The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election.

Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues.

  • An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning.
  • Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions.
  • "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said.

Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days, after barely speaking for many weeks.

  • A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre."
  • The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said.
  • Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday.
  • If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating.
  • The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first.
  • They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third.

Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation.

  • A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

item.title: Student protest unrest spreads across Europe
item.description:
Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France.

Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions.

Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding.

  • There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France.
  • In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1.

The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education.

In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews, including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations.

In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France."

  • Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports.

In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ.

In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau.

In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports.

Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service.

  • France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts.
  • That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending.

The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns.

Go deeper: The global fiscal reckoning is here
